case_studies.action: Ledgerglass matched supported rows, added three statement overlays, and left one uncertain provider row out of the effective cycle.
case_studies.difficulty: The balance was real, but the transaction feed could not explain it.
case_studies.happened: A connected credit card stopped including several posted purchases near the end of a closed cycle.
case_studies.reversal: A later exact provider transaction replaces its overlay without deleting the statement observation.
case_studies.title: The feed missed three purchases
case_studies.uncertainty: The uncertain row remains visible for later provider or owner evidence.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass kept the connected statement and provider rows together, left all provider rows posted, and created an explainable owner-review ambiguity without adding an overlay or exclusion.
case_studies.difficulty: Choosing the first identifier would make a deterministic result look authoritative while hiding a real one-to-many collision.
evidence: exact amount, date, and text factors
case_studies.happened: One row on a complete synthetic statement had the same amount, calendar date, and normalized text as two posted provider rows.
case_studies.reversal: An atomic evidence-bound owner decision can close the whole component only after excess activity is handled. A later provider arrival refreshes a deficient component; invalidated assignments reopen for safe reassignment while immutable review history remains intact.
case_studies.title: Two exact rows were not one answer
case_studies.uncertainty: The cycle remains partial until independent evidence supports one distinct active provider for every connected statement row and resolves every excess active candidate. The invariant applies to every connected ambiguity, not only exact-text collisions; equal-count interchangeable duplicates can still match one-to-one.

case_studies.action: After the policy window, Ledgerglass marked it expired-assumed and removed it from operational totals.
case_studies.difficulty: Absence does not prove cancellation, and counting it forever overstates spending.
case_studies.happened: A pending grocery authorization disappeared from later provider responses.
case_studies.reversal: A fresh observation reactivates it; a unique posted match settles it.
case_studies.title: A pending purchase vanished
case_studies.uncertainty: Expired-assumed is reversible bookkeeping, not a cancellation claim.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass gave derived records source-backed identity references, preserved existing evidence, and used the counted projection for reconciliation and operational totals. Enrichment and confirmed relationships now affect the second provider's effective rows and search revisions.
case_studies.difficulty: Copying those transactions into a manual source would hide the broken reference contract and risk counting them twice.
evidence: authentic provider account and transaction identities
case_studies.happened: A fictional household activated an account supplied only by its second provider. Reads included the account, but reconciliation could not persist because derived records still required first-provider ledger identities.
case_studies.reversal: Pausing contribution hides current counted evidence without deleting historical identities. Changed source or relationship evidence invalidates dependent search revisions.
case_studies.title: A counted account also needs working reconciliation
case_studies.uncertainty: Working persistence does not prove financial completeness. Missing statement evidence and ambiguous relationships remain unresolved.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass confirmed only a unique exact assignment and attached the Plaid observation to the existing canonical event without adding another counted transaction.
case_studies.difficulty: Blindly importing both rows would double spending, while matching by amount and date alone could collapse two legitimate same-day purchases.
case_studies.happened: A fictional SimpleFIN account and a Plaid Sandbox account both reported the same posted coffee purchase.
case_studies.reversal: An append-only unmerge decision restores singleton consensus while retaining every candidate observation and prior decision.
case_studies.title: Two providers saw one coffee purchase
case_studies.uncertainty: Repeated equal purchases, merchant drift, and date drift remain explicit review candidates; account or currency conflicts are prohibited.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass paired the incremental transaction stream with the provider's complete cached account snapshot and recorded the account's balance evidence under the same successful attempt.
case_studies.difficulty: Treating a transaction cursor as the account inventory would silently omit the account and leave its activated balance out of the canonical projection.
case_studies.happened: A fictional provider shared a newly opened checking account whose incremental transaction response was empty.
case_studies.reversal: Contribution can be paused without deleting the provider observation; a later authentic snapshot appends newer evidence.
case_studies.title: A new account had a balance but no new transactions
case_studies.uncertainty: The cached balance is dated provider evidence, not a real-time claim. No historical observation is synthesized from mutable state.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass created one continuity discrepancy with the required adjacent-statement evidence and a deterministic resolution condition.
case_studies.difficulty: Arithmetic inside each document could pass while the missing movement between cycles stayed unexplained.
case_studies.happened: Two synthetic card statements each balanced internally, but the next opening balance was different from the prior closing balance.
case_studies.reversal: A corrected statement version can supersede the effective evidence; the old version and discrepancy history remain auditable.
case_studies.title: Two correct statements still did not connect
case_studies.uncertainty: No balancing transaction is invented and the difference remains waiting or owner-review work.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass promoted an account-scoped exact rule after checking affected rows.
case_studies.difficulty: A broad text rule would also change unrelated merchants and contaminate evaluation rows.
case_studies.happened: A noisy merchant string was repeatedly categorized as shopping instead of a subscription.
case_studies.reversal: A later authoritative contradiction suspends the rule and restores field provenance.
case_studies.title: A correction became a narrow rule
case_studies.uncertainty: The rule applies only to its proven scope.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass kept current evidence usable and attached precise coverage warnings to affected answers.
case_studies.difficulty: A single stale source should not turn known balances into invented totals or make every tool unusable.
case_studies.happened: One synthetic institution stopped refreshing while the other connections stayed current.
case_studies.reversal: The next authenticated observation clears the stale condition without rewriting history.
case_studies.title: One connection went stale
case_studies.uncertainty: Any total containing the stale account is explicitly partial.

case_studies.action: The steward queued derived work independently of sync. Owner-requested recovery returns an acceptance receipt and runs a bounded durable pass with stage checkpoints, rather than waiting for model work inside the request. A resumed run preserves terminal failure receipts.
case_studies.difficulty: Retrying the whole sync could duplicate work while leaving the actual failed stage unclear.
case_studies.happened: A vector-index write timed out after a successful transaction sync.
case_studies.reversal: Derived artifacts can be rebuilt from the canonical ledger.
case_studies.title: The ledger was right but search was behind
case_studies.uncertainty: Acceptance does not prove completion. Semantic search stays incomplete until recovery succeeds, and omitted source-lifecycle work remains outstanding for scheduled recovery. A latest-run status must match the accepted run before it can establish that request's outcome.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass kept committed, expected, and possible paths separate, expanded occurrences deterministically, and kept each currency on its own account path.
case_studies.difficulty: Treating all three as equally certain would make the next balance look more precise than the evidence allows.
case_studies.happened: A synthetic household had a confirmed card payment, a statement-supported bill, and a recurring purchase pattern with no fixed amount.
case_studies.reversal: Schedules and occurrence states are append-only derived expectations; changing an assumption creates a new revision without changing ledger evidence.
case_studies.title: The future was a range, not a number
case_studies.uncertainty: The possible path is a scenario range, not a probability or a promise; missing balances and stale terms remain visible as coverage warnings.

case_studies.action: Ledgerglass kept the transfer classification and exposed the model output only as rejected derived evidence.
case_studies.difficulty: The prose was plausible, but it conflicted with a confirmed transfer relationship.
case_studies.happened: A model confidently described a card payment as ordinary spending.
case_studies.reversal: A confirmed owner correction can replace the relationship through the normal audited path.
case_studies.title: The model sounded sure and was still wrong
case_studies.uncertainty: Narrative confidence never outranks transaction relationships.
